en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Book of Puzzles,
Chapter on the Power of Psychic Success.
1. The Fruitful Question on Duties Performed Then King Milinda, having been granted leave, prostrated at the feet of the venerable one, placed his joined palms to his head, and said this:
“Venerable Nāgasena, these sectarians say thus:”

‘If the Buddha accepts worship, then the Buddha has not attained final Nibbāna; he is bound to the world, still within existence, and common to the world. Therefore, any service rendered to him is not barren but bears fruit.
If, however, he has attained final Nibbāna, is detached from the world, and has emerged from all states of existence, then no worship accrues to him;
having attained final Nibbāna, he accepts nothing, and any service rendered to one who accepts nothing is barren and fruitless. This is a dilemma from both sides.
“This question is not within the domain of those who have not attained the mind; it is the domain of the great ones alone. Tear asunder this net of views and set it aside!
This question has come to you; grant the eye of wisdom to the future sons of the Conqueror for the purpose of refuting the arguments of others.
The Elder said:

“The Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna, Great King, yet the Blessed One does not accept offerings. Even at the foot of the Bodhi tree, the Tathāgata’s acceptance of offerings was abandoned; how much more so now that he has attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna without residue?
This was also said, Great King, by the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma:
‘When those who are unequaled are being honored, ...’”
“Even by gods and humans together,
they do not accept honor;
this is the natural law of the Buddhas.”
The King said:
"Venerable Nāgasena, a son may speak in praise of his father, or a father may speak in praise of his son;
yet this is not a reason for the refutation of opposing doctrines, for it is merely a manifestation of one's own faith. Pray, explain that to me."
“Give the correct reason for establishing your own doctrine and for unraveling the web of views.
The Elder said:
“The Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna, Great King, and the Blessed One does not accept offerings; yet even though the Tathāgata does not accept them...”
“Devas and humans, making the jewel of the relics their foundation and practicing right conduct with the Tathāgata’s jewel of wisdom as their object, obtain the three kinds of success.
Great King, suppose a vast, great mass of fire were to blaze up and then go out; would that great mass of fire, Great King, consent to the fuel of grass and wood? “No, indeed, Blessed One.”
“Venerable sir, even while burning, that great mass of fire does not accept the fuel of grass and wood; how much less would it, when extinguished, calmed, and insentient, accept anything?
“But, Great King, when that mass of fire has ceased and is calmed, is there fire left in the world?
“No indeed, venerable sir. Wood is the basis and the fuel for fire; those people who desire fire—”
“By means of their own strength, power, and energy, through personal human effort, they rub the wood together, produce fire, and perform with that fire the tasks to be accomplished by fire.
“In that case, Great King, the statement of the sectarians is false: ‘An act performed for one who does not consent becomes barren and fruitless.’”
Just as, O Great King, a vast and great mass of fire blazes up,
even so did the Blessed One blaze forth with the splendor of a Buddha throughout the ten-thousandfold world system.
Just as, O Great King, that vast and great mass of fire, having blazed up, is extinguished;
In the same way, the Blessed One, having blazed with the glory of a Buddha throughout the ten-thousandfold world system, has attained final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue.
Just as, O Great King, a mass of fire that has been extinguished no longer accepts fuel in the form of grass and wood,
even so the acceptance of worldly things has been abandoned and stilled by him who is for the welfare of the world.
Just as, great king, when a mass of fire has gone out, men— by their own strength, power, and energy,
through personal human effort— might rub together wood to produce fire and, by means of that fire, perform the tasks to be done with fire; even so, O gods and humans,
[they take] the jewel of the relics of the Tathāgata who has attained final Nibbāna, even though he does not consent to it.
Taking the Tathāgata as their object, those who practice the right path by taking the jewel of the Tathāgata’s knowledge as their focal point obtain the three kinds of success;
for this reason too, Great King, a service rendered to the Tathāgata, even though he has attained final Nibbāna and does not personally accept it,
becomes not barren but fruitful.
"Furthermore, Great King, hear another superior reason why a service rendered to a Tathāgata who has attained final Nibbāna—even though he does not consent—is never barren but becomes fruitful.
Just as, Great King, a great and mighty wind might blow and then cease; would that ceased wind, Great King, consent to being produced again?
"No indeed, Bhante; there is no intention or mental attention on the part of the ceased wind toward being produced again."
“What is the reason?
“Because that wind-element is insentient.
“Great King, when that wind has ceased, does the designation ‘wind’ disappear?”

“No, venerable sir, palm-leaf fans and whisks are not conditions for the arising of wind. Rather, those people who are oppressed by heat and afflicted by fever generate that wind through their own strength, power, and energy, and by means of personal human effort;
with that wind, they cool the heat and allay the fever.”
“In that case, Great King, the statement of the sectarians is false, namely: ‘An act performed for one who does not consent is barren and fruitless.
Just as, Great King, a great, mighty wind blows, even so the Blessed One blew with the cool, sweet, peaceful, and subtle breeze of loving-kindness throughout the ten-thousandfold world system.”
Just as, Great King, a great and mighty wind, having blown, ceases;
even so the Blessed One, having blown with the wind of loving-kindness—cool, sweet, peaceful, and subtle—is fully extinguished in the element of nibbāna without residue.
Just as, Great King, the ceased wind does not admit of being produced again; [so it is with the Blessed One].
In the same way, the delighting in worldly things has been abandoned and stilled for one who works for the welfare of the world.
Great King, just as those people were scorched by heat and oppressed by feverish distress,
even so are gods and humans oppressed by the feverish distress of the threefold fire of suffering.
Just as palm-leaf fans and whisks are conditions for the production of wind,
even so the relics of the Tathāgata and the jewel of his knowledge are conditions for the attainment of the three kinds of excellence.
Just as people, tormented by heat and oppressed by feverish distress, produce wind with a palm-leaf fan or a whisk and thereby extinguish the heat and allay the feverish distress;

In the same way, O Great King, when the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, gods and humans—without his even accepting it—worship both his relics and the jewel of his wisdom; having generated merit, they extinguish and pacify the burning heat of the threefold fire by means of that merit.
For this reason also, O Great King, any service rendered to the Tathāgata who has attained final Nibbāna, though he does not accept it, becomes fruitful and productive.
Furthermore, O Great King, listen to another superior argument for the refutation of opposing views.
“Suppose, great king, a man were to strike a drum and produce a sound.
That sound produced by the man would then vanish. Would that sound, great king, consent to being produced again?

“No, venerable sir. Once that sound has vanished, there is no intention or mental application for its re-arising; once the sound of the drum has been produced and has vanished, that drum-sound is utterly cut off.”
“But, venerable sir, the drum is a condition for the production of sound; then, when the condition exists, a person produces the sound by striking the drum with an effort of his own.

“In the same way, great king, the Blessed One—having established the Teacher who is perfected in virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, as well as the jewel of the elements, the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the instruction—himself [entered] the state without remainder...”
He has attained final Nibbāna in the element of Nibbāna; yet, even though the Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna, the attainment of prosperity has not been cut off.

Beings oppressed by the suffering of existence, making the jewel of the relics, the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the instruction their support, being desirous of prosperity, obtain prosperities. For this reason too, Great King—
“Even when the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, a service performed—even if he does not personally accept it—becomes fruitful and productive.
This, Great King, was seen by the Blessed One regarding the future time;
it was declared, spoken, and explained: ‘It may be, Ānanda, that you think thus: “The Teacher is past away.”’”
‘We have no Teacher; the word of the Teacher no longer exists’—Ānanda, you should not view it thus.
‘The Dhamma and Vinaya, Ānanda, which have been taught and laid down by me, shall be your teacher after my passing.
When the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna and does not accept [anything further], any service rendered becomes barren and fruitless.
That speech of those sectarians is false, unreal, untrue, incorrect, contradictory,
perverted, productive of suffering, resulting in suffering, and leading to states of deprivation. Furthermore, O Great King,
hear another further reason why an offering made to a Tathāgata who has attained final Nibbāna— even though he does not accept it— becomes fruitful and not in vain.
“Does this great earth, O Great King, consent: ‘Let all seeds grow upon me’?
“No, venerable sir.

“But why, O Great King, do those seeds, though the great earth does not consent, sprout and become firmly established with deep roots and a network of fibers, with trunks, cores, and branches spreading out, bearing flowers and fruits?”
“Even though the great earth, venerable sir, does not seek them out, it serves as the site for those seeds and provides the condition for their growth;
supported by that site and conditioned by that, those seeds grow forth, becoming firmly established with deep-rooted fibers,
spreading wide with trunks, cores, and branches, and bearing flowers and fruits.”
“In that case, Great King, the followers of other sects have been defeated, destroyed, and contradicted within their own doctrines. If they should say,
‘An act performed for one who does not consent becomes barren and fruitless,’ then,
Great King, just as the great earth is, so is the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
Just as, Great King, the great earth does not accept anything, so the Tathāgata does not accept anything.

Just as, Great King, those seeds, having sprouted depending on the earth, become firmly established with deep-rooted fibers, spreading out with trunks, cores, and branches, and bearing flowers and fruits; even so, Great King, gods and humans [depend] upon the Tathāgata.
Even though he has attained final Nibbāna and does not accept anything, by relying upon both his relics and the jewel of his knowledge,

[the offerings] become firmly established upon the roots of merit, possess the trunk of concentration, the branches of the essential Dharma, and bear the flowers of liberation and the fruits of the ascetic life; for this reason also, Great King,
a service rendered to the Tathāgata who has attained final Nibbāna and does not accept anything is truly effective.
"It becomes non-wasteful and fruitful.
Furthermore, Great King, hear another superior reason why an act performed toward a Tathāgata who has attained final Nibbāna—even though he does not accept it—becomes non-wasteful and fruitful.
"Do these camels, oxen, donkeys, goats, cattle, or humans, Great King, consent to the arising of swarms of worms within their bellies?"
“No, venerable sir.
“But why, great king, did those worms develop within the bellies of those beings who did not consent, and why did they reach such abundance with many sons and grandsons?
“Because of the power of evil karma, venerable sir, worms developed within the bellies of those very beings who did not consent, and they reached such abundance with many sons and grandsons.”

“In the same way, Great King, even though the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna and does not accept [the offering], because of the power of the relics and the object of knowledge, a service rendered to the Tathāgata becomes fruitful and productive.
Furthermore, Great King, hear another further reason why a service rendered to the Tathāgata who has attained final Nibbāna and does not accept it becomes fruitful and productive.
Do these people, Great King, consent to these ninety-eight diseases arising in their bodies?”
“No indeed, Bhante.
“But why, Great King, do diseases fall upon your body when you do not consent to them?
“By evil conduct performed in the past, Bhante.”

“If, Great King, unwholesome karma performed in the past is to be experienced here [in this life], then indeed, Great King, wholesome and unwholesome karma—whether performed in the past or performed here—is unfailing and bears fruit.
For this reason too, Great King, an act of service rendered toward a Tathāgata who has attained final Nibbāna, even though he no longer accepts it, is unfailing and bears fruit.
Have you not heard before, Great King, how the yakkha named Nandaka, having assailed the Elder Sāriputta, sank into the earth?”
“Yes, venerable sir, it is heard; this is well known in the world.
“But did the elder Sāriputta consent, Great King, to the great earth-sinking of the yakkha Nandaka?

“Venerable sir, even if the world with its devas were torn asunder, even if the sun and moon were to fall to the ground, even if Sineru, the king of mountains, were to be scattered, the elder Sāriputta would not consent to the suffering of another.”
For what reason?
Because that cause by which the elder Sāriputta might become angry or resentful has been completely uprooted and severed for the elder Sāriputta;
because that cause has been eradicated, venerable sir, even toward one who would take his life, the elder Sāriputta—
“He should not have become angry.
“If, Great King, the Elder Sāriputta did not consent to the earth-sinking of the yakkha Nandaka, why then did the yakkha Nandaka enter the earth?
“Because of the power of unwholesome karma, venerable sir.”
“If, Great King, because of the power of an unwholesome deed the yakkha Nandaka entered the earth, then an offense committed—even against one who does not consent—becomes non-vain and fruitful.
Therefore, Great King, because of the power of even an unwholesome deed, an act performed against one who does not consent becomes non-vain and fruitful.
For this reason also, Great King, an act performed against the Tathāgata after he has attained final nibbāna—even though he does not consent—becomes non-vain and fruitful.”
“Great King, how many people are there now who have entered this great earth, and is their voice heard there?
“Yes, venerable sir, it is heard.
“Come now, Great King, let them speak.”
“Venerable sir, Ciñcā the maidservant, Suppabuddha the Sakyan, the elder Devadatta, the yakkha Nandaka, and the young brahmin Nanda— venerable sir,
I have heard that these five persons have entered the great earth.
“By what fault, Great King, were they offended?”
“And with regard to the Blessed One and his disciples, venerable sir?
“Now, Great King, did the Blessed One or his disciples approve of this sinking into the great earth?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“Therefore, Great King, even though the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna and does not accept it, a service rendered to him becomes not barren but fruitful.
“Excellent, Bhante Nāgasena! This profound question has been well explained; what was deep has been made clear, the hidden has been revealed, the knot has been untied, the thicket has been made open.
The arguments of opponents have perished, false views have been shattered, and the rival sectarians have been deprived of their luster.”
“Having relied upon you, the most excellent among the best of the assembly.
Thus ends the first question: “The Fruit of Performed Merit.”
